CALDWELL — Canyon County needs a new jail to replace its existing Dale G. Haile Detention Center, which was built in 1991 and opened in 1993. Just ask the people who work there.

![Canyon County Jail Tour](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahopress.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/a/3c/a3c68e78-50a7-40b6-94fa-2321305c277a/69ebf380aa259.image.jpg)

Capt. Harold Patchett, with the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office, holds open the door leading to the intake area of the Dale G. Haile Detention Center, Wednesday, April, 22, 2026.

Joe Decker, public information officer for Canyon County Sheriff’s Office, spoke to the Idaho Press on Friday night about what’s holding back a new county jail.

“Funding is the biggest hurdle to getting a new jail built,” Decker said. “Rather than helping counties find additional revenue streams to help with that, the legislature has refused to even look at or discuss a solution like a local option tax.”

According to Decker, the county has been trying to get funding since 2006. It tried for a bond five times. He said the jail bond nearly passed by a simple majority in both 2006 and 2009 but needs a two-thirds supermajority, which is an even higher bar to pass.

Decker said they’ve tried to lobby for a 1 cent local option sales tax. But to do so, the state Legislature would have to pass a bill to allow Canyon County residents to vote on creating such a tax.

“We even sweetened the pot with some proposed legislation,” Decker said. “Half of that cent would go to property tax relief, the other half-cent would go to the jail build.”

The issues inside all start with booking, according to Harold Patchett, captain for the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office. Patchett led the Idaho Press on a tour of the jail.

This is part one in a two-part series about the jail and the county’s need for a new one.

About 150 workers lead the “24-7 operation,” according to Patchett.

“Booking is our major hub, everything runs through booking,” Patchett said to the Idaho Press during a jail tour. “All of our courts and transports run everything through here, so if they’re coming down to court, or going to (other) places. All of our medical happens down here, so whenever we have patients waiting to see medical, they have to be staged here.”

Patchett mentioned inmates with wheelchairs, crutches or canes, or any other kind of medical issue are housed in booking.

The problem is it overloads the staff in that area.

“We turned this from a section that books people in to a massive hub of people and different situations that are going on,” Patchett said. “It’s very difficult to manage as there is so much going on down here, and we just don’t have anywhere else to put (inmates with) medical needs (and) mental health needs.”

The booking area is about the size of a small hotel lobby. On a busy night, there are probably three to seven employees — from the arresting officer, to the deputies and the support staff, Decker said.

The range of employees in booking is a “fluid situation,” because it depends on who is being brought in — someone who was arrested for driving under the influence and is cooperating, or someone who is agitated or violent in some way, Decker said.

Booking is also where jail staff processes new inmates. Among the tasks Patchett listed are fingerprinting, photos and a classification assessment for their housing situations — placing inmates with other inmates who have committed similar classes of crime and have the same sex and special needs. And then, there are inmates who need a “cool down period,” or they’re detoxing from drugs.

The intake period slowdown, because of all the extra tasks booking needs to do, “can be significant,” according to Patchett.

“If you took a look at the quantity of disturbances that we have, most of them are centered here in booking, which also means they’re stopping everything in the booking process to deal with whatever that disturbance is,” Patchett said.

He said “on average,” jail staff can usually clear someone through booking in one to two hours.

![Canyon County Jail Tour](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahopress.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/9/92/992476b9-dea4-456c-941e-36df33f97851/69ebf38ad0b71.image.jpg)

Deputies with the Canyon County Sheriff's Office gather in the booking area at the Dale G. Haile Detention Center, Wednesday, April, 22, 2026.

“Depending on what’s happening and what the needs are from the housing section here, it could slow that process down to half a day,” Patchett said. “So then we end up having everybody just stashed in one of our holding cells, waiting to be processed, because it’s just too busy.”

While the jail doesn’t track who has mental health issues on top of the charges they’re facing, jail staff said mental health issues are “definitely on the rise.”

The jail also uses fingerprinting, mugshots and a retinal scanner to further verify their identities.

“You can’t change your eye very easily,” Patchett said.

One advanced piece of technology is something the jail received in 2022. It’s a full-body scanner that is similar to what is used at airports. It’s called the Tek84 body scanner. The scanner “delivers clear visibility of contraband hidden on and inside the body,” [Tek84](https://www.tek84.com/intercept) states.

![Canyon County Jail Tour](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahopress.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/f/2b/f2be5679-7b2b-4783-902b-95eb483c56d5/69ebf3831f2c3.image.jpg)

The first room an inmate walks into a the Canyon County Jail is dominated by a Tek84 full body scanner, used to make sure inmates are not carrying anything into the facility, Wednesday, April, 22, 2026.

The jail also has reverse airflow cells for inmates who may have an illness such as tuberculosis or some sort of airborne, contagious disease.

“We put them in there and it sucks the air out,” Patchett said. “That way, we’re not breathing the same air.”

The inmates are also changed out of their clothing, showered, supplied orange jail clothing and sent to their living unit, Patchett said.

![Canyon County Jail Tour](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahopress.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/9/f8/9f8c708d-4f9d-47cb-a28b-9043072a0ba2/69ebf38f9978d.image.jpg)

Inmates are changed out of their clothing, showered, and supplied orange jail clothing before they are sent to their living unit at the Dale G. Haile Detention Center, Wednesday, April, 22, 2026.

In addition to all that goes down in booking, the kitchen is full-service.

“We serve roughly 505-550 meals three times a day,” Patchett said. “This kitchen also feeds the juvenile (inmates) across the street.”

![Canyon County Jail Tour](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahopress.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/b/c5/bc56d2b4-c8e8-4c9f-88c1-22b127c0917d/69ebf392abd4c.image.jpg)

The kitchen area of what is said to be "the largest restaurant in Canyon County" at the Dale G. Haile Detention Center, Wednesday, April, 22, 2026.

Canyon County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Russ Donnelly said “they say we’re the largest restaurant in Canyon County.”

In addition to working on the menu and organizing the meals, the private contractor Summit Food Services also prepares meals for the jail’s deputies.

“That way our deputies don’t have to go out and find food,” Patchett said, noting it helps keep the deputies at work in case there are any problems that occur during meal time.

![Canyon County Jail Tour -](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahopress.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/0/da/0da4bb7d-c0b6-4ded-81ee-006cdf5c9c31/69ebf3a52a2e9.image.jpg)

Capt. Harold Patchett, with the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office, looks into a cell pod prior to lunch being served at the Dale G. Haile Detention Center, Wednesday, April 22, 2026.

According to Patchett, the jail categorizes its inmates in several ways — current charges, previous charges, male, female, any behavioral issues within the jail.

All of that is before the different living pods and units where offenders of many different levels live. One of those units is Pod 1, which houses Unit A, where the jail’s worst offenders live. Welcome to Canyon County Jail.

**Matthew Neil Wells** is the Nampa reporter at the Idaho Press. He covers city government, crime, features, profiles on people, and events. You can follow him on X @MatthewNWells, and email him at [mwells@idahopress.com](mailto:mwells@idahopress.com).
